message.content:
Lions (Panthera leo) belong to the order **Carnivora** (family Felidae), while zebras (Equus quagga) belong to the order **Perissodactyla** (family Equidae).  
The two lineages split very early in mammalian evolution, during the Paleocene (about 65–70 million years ago).  

So the **last common ancestor of a lion and a zebra was a small, insect‑eating mammal that lived in the Paleocene and gave rise to the two major groups that would later become the carnivores and the odd‑toed ungulates**. In other words, it is the last common ancestor of the orders Carnivora and Perissodactyla, and ultimately of all placental mammals.

The user asks: "What is the common ancestor of lion and zebra?" They want a biological answer. The common ancestor of lion (Panthera leo) and zebra (Equus quagga) would be a common ancestor in the mammalian lineage. Both are mammals, but lions are felids (family Felidae), zebras are equids (family Equidae). They diverged from a common ancestor in the order Carnivora vs Perissodactyla? Actually lions are in order Carnivora, suborder Feliformia. Zebras are in order Perissodactyla (odd-toed ungulates). So their common ancestor would be a more distant mammalian ancestor, perhaps a common ancestor of all placental mammals (Eutheria). But maybe the question expects "the common ancestor of lion and zebra is a mammal that lived around 100 million years ago" or "the common ancestor is a mammal that gave rise to both the carnivores and perissodactyls." The common ancestor of the two species is the last common ancestor of the families Felidae and Equidae, which is the last common ancestor of the orders Carnivora and Perissodactyla. That would be a mammal from the Paleocene or early Eocene. The last common ancestor of all placental mammals is the "Eutherian ancestor" that lived about 65-100 million years ago. But the last common ancestor of the two orders might be older. The divergence between the two lineages likely occurred in the Paleocene (~66-56 million years ago). So the common ancestor would be a small, insectivorous mammal. But the question might be answered simply: "The common ancestor of lion and zebra is a mammal that lived around 100 million years ago, the last common ancestor of all placental mammals." Or "the common ancestor is a mammal that gave rise to both the carnivores and perissodactyls." The user didn't specify the level of detail. So we can answer: "The last common ancestor of lions and zebras is a small, insectivorous mammal that lived in the Paleocene, roughly 65-70 million years ago, which is the last common ancestor of the orders Carnivora and Perissodactyla." Or we can mention "the last common ancestor of all placental mammals" if we want to be more general.
